97... ## Outcome vocabulary
98... 
99... Every task resolves to one **outcome**. Read-only detection (the resolver seeing a status source satisfied) and the `transition_status(status='advance', outcome=…)` write speak the same vocabulary:
100... 
101... | Outcome | Meaning |
102... |---|---|
103... | `completed` | The task finished successfully. |
104... | `failed` | The task could not finish; carries an `error` class (below). Routes into the fix loop, or the errored bucket. |
105... | `excluded` | The task was disabled for this project/object (see [How to exclude a task](#how-to-exclude-a-task)); the machine follows the task's `excluded` branch. |
106... | `skipped` | Deferred for now (not disabled) — the task may still run later. |
107... | `inProgress` | The task has started but has not completed. It remains the current blocking task. |
108... 
109... **`error` classes** (required on `failed`):
110... 
111... | Class | Use for |
112... |---|---|
113... | `sql` | A SQL/DDL bug the fix loop can address. |
114... | `infra` | A transient environment failure (timeout, connection drop, cancelled run) — retry with `reset`. |
115... | `data` | Set by the plugin, not by hand: a `validateData` run finished with mismatches. The walk stops there; resolve it with re-validation or a data/mapping fix, not the fix loop. |
116... | `human` | Only a person can resolve it. Don't set this class by hand — call `transition_status(status='escalate', task=…, asks=[…])`, which sets it for you. Passing `outcome='failed'` without an error class instead sends the object into the fix loop, where no code change resolves it. A judgment you *can* make is `status='note'` (does not park; review later), not this class. |
117... 
118... ## Per-task contracts
119... 
120... Every entry below names the task id, what your override needs as input, and the signal that tells the plugin the task is complete. "Done when" is the only completion contract — once the listed condition holds, the plugin moves on.
121... 
122... > **Signaling completion.** After the work, call `transition_status(status='advance', task='<task_id>', outcome=…)` so `TASK_EVENTS` get an `advanced` row — do not leave completion to `migration_status` / `next_task` alone when an oracle already looks done. For agent and mcpTool tasks, also call `transition_status(status='started', task=…, where=…)` once at skill entry (MCP tools separately emit `mcp_tool_started` / `mcp_tool_returned` around the tool call). The plugin still reads the "Done when" condition (registry field, file on disk, Snowflake object, job progress) to confirm; completed advances without a registry stamp are allowed when that oracle confirms and refused when it disagrees. Use `advance` for failures, judged outcomes, and overrides (`bypass` / `reset` / `skip`) as well. A registry-field "Done when" reads completed when `status = 'completed'` (or when the field exists, if it has no `status`).

124... > **Signaling completion via session config.** Setup tasks that gather user choices complete by calling the `configure` MCP tool with the relevant field set (e.g. `configure(source_language='sqlserver')`). The plugin reads from the session config to know the task is done.

126... > **ETL route selection.** Missing `etl_flow` and `etl_flow=stabilize`

287... ## Custom code units (`kind=custom`)
288... 
289... Per-task overrides and custom machines are about **how** work runs. Custom code units are about **what** work runs on. The conversion engine generates a known set of object kinds (tables, views, procedures, functions, SSIS packages, …); anything outside that — orchestration tools (FiveTran, Airflow, Informatica), BI assets (SSAS cubes, Tableau extracts, dbt models), object kinds the engine doesn't generate yet (Oracle PACKAGE bodies, SQL Server triggers in some flows), or hand-maintained scripts — won't show up in the registry unless you put it there yourself.
290... 
291... The registry's top-level `kind` is a closed enum with four values: `"databaseObject"`, `"script"`, `"etl"` (the three the conversion engine emits) and `"custom"` (everything else). Custom units carry an additional `customKind` discriminator on `source` and `target` — that's the free-form string the agent uses to group, filter, and route. Each custom unit carries:
292... 
293... - **`kind`** — always `"custom"` for these units. The closed enum keeps registry queries and bindings simple.
294... - **`source.customKind` / `target.customKind`** — the free-form discriminator (`"fivetran"`, `"ssasCube"`, `"oraclePackage"`, `"airflowDag"`, …). Pick a stable name; this is what `query_registry where="source.customKind = '<x>'"` filters on. Cannot be one of the four reserved Kind values.
295... - **`source.name`** — display name.
296... - **`source.objectType`** — *optional*. When the asset maps cleanly to a built-in `ObjectType` (e.g. an Oracle PACKAGE → `package`), set it so the unit groups with its siblings in `migration_status`. `"other"` is fine when nothing fits.
297... - **`files.source.path`** — *optional* path to a config file or definition, **relative to the project root** (e.g. `"source/fivetran/orders_sync/connector.py"`). Assets living outside the project must be copied under `<project_dir>/source/` first; an absolute or escaping path is reported in `warnings[]` because it breaks for every other checkout.
298... - **`dependencies.dependsOn[]`** — ids of other units (built-in or custom) this one reads/writes. `requiredBy` back-edges and `planning.topologicalRank` are derived from this by the registry on every write — never hand-write either.
299... - **`extensions.machine`** — name of the state machine that drives this unit, as a plain string. Only the four compiled-in machines resolve (`main`, `setup`, `data-migration-setup`, `data-validation-setup`); see the gap note below. When unset or unresolvable, a `.scai/skills/<customKind>.md` skill (if present) replaces `main`; otherwise the unit walks `main`.
300... 
301... ### Registering custom units
302... 
303... One tool, `register_units`, three shapes. Search that name if the tool is not already loaded — there is no `register_custom_unit` / `register_custom_units_from_manifest`.
304... 
305... | Shape | Call | When |
306... |---|---|---|
307... | One unit | `register_units(custom_kind, name, ...)` | Walking the user through one item. |
308... | A list | `register_units(entries=[...])` | Manifest with many entries (CSV/JSON/YAML the user has on hand). |
309... | Findings | `register_units(expected_slugs=[...])` | Investigation agents already wrote `.scai/tmp/extras/findings/<slug>.json`. |
310... 
311... It rejects the four reserved Kind values (`databaseObject`, `script`, `etl`, `custom`) as a `customKind`. Built-in kinds go through the regular `scai code add` / `scai code extract` paths. Per-row failures are collected into `failed[]` rather than aborting the run.
312... 
313... Snake_case (`custom_kind`, `source_path`, `depends_on`, `expected_slugs`) and camelCase (`customKind`, `sourcePath`, `dependsOn`, `expectedSlugs`) both work. `dependsOn` takes either a JSON array of ids or a comma/newline-separated string.
314... 
315... Every shape returns the same envelope — `registered[]` (each row has `id`, `customKind`, `name`, `machine`, `dependsOnResolved`, `dependsOnMissing`, `warnings`) plus `failed[]` / `withMissingDependencies[]` / `withWarnings[]`. Read `dependsOnMissing`: ids in it are recorded but match no unit, which is expected when the dependency is registered later and a typo otherwise. Read `warnings`: an unresolvable machine name (unit uses a `.scai/skills/<customKind>.md` skill if present, otherwise `main`) or a `sourcePath` that isn't repo-relative. Don't re-query to confirm the write — `query_registry`'s default projection is `id` / `source` / `files`, so `dependencies` and `extensions` come back absent and the unit looks empty. Pass `fields=["*"]` if you do need to read them back.
316... 
317... Investigation fans out; the write does not. Investigation agents write one JSON fragment each under `.scai/tmp/extras/findings/<slug>.json`. The orchestrator calls `register_units(expected_slugs=[...])`, which merges those files and registers — it does not concatenate fragments in context. Registry writes take an exclusive lock and each triggers a registry-wide graph refresh, so parallel writes from the agents themselves are slower than one batch and fragment the failure report.
318... 
319... ### Per-customKind skills
320... 
321... Discovery writes `<project_dir>/.scai/skills/<customKind>.md` with the customer (one cookbook per kind, reused for every object of that kind). When that file exists, those units skip `main` (register → convert → …) and run the skill as their whole workflow. Completion is the same stamp `verify` already uses:
322... 
323... ```
324... transition_status(status='advance', task='verify', outcome='completed', where="id IN ('<id>')")
325... ```
326... 
327... Done when `extensions.tasks.verify` reads completed. `next_objects` / `next_task` carry `skillPath` pointing at the file. The file must be a procedure (On Entry → steps → stamp); see `setup/discover-extras/cookbook-template.md`.
328... 
329... A loaded `extensions.machine` still wins when that name is compiled in. A `verify/SKILL.md` task override does not steal these units.
330... 
331... ### Gap: per-customKind machines are not implemented
332... 
333... `Machines` loads only the four machines compiled into the server. Nothing reads `<project_dir>/.scai/machines/`, so a machine file written there is inert, and `extensions.machine` naming it resolves to nothing — `machine_for_unit` then uses a `.scai/skills/<customKind>.md` skill if present, otherwise `main`.
334... 
335... Consequences to keep in mind when extending this area:
336... 
337... - Don't author a per-`customKind` machine file and report the flow as wired. The fallback is silent at resolve time; the only signals are `warnings[]` on each `registered[]` row (`withWarnings[]` on the `register_units` report) and the `Warning:` line from `update_registry(field="extensions.machine", ...)`.
338... - The executor kinds are `mcpTool`, `shell`, and `agent`. There is no `manual` kind and no `instructions` field — a machine using them fails to deserialize, which is a second reason a hand-written machine never takes effect.
339... - Making this real means loading and validating `.scai/machines/*.json` into `by_name` alongside the built-ins, and threading `project_dir` into the ~15 `Machines::load_builtin()` call sites. That's a feature, not a doc fix.
340... 
341... ### Invoking discovery
342... 
343... The skill at `setup/discover-extras/SKILL.md` registers the units, then co-authors a `.scai/skills/<customKind>.md` cookbook per kind with the customer. Load it when the user has extras to register — it is not a step in the compiled `setup` machine.
344... 
345... Re-entering the skill at any time afterward is safe — it picks up where the user left off and lets them add more units.
346... 
347... ### Worked example: FiveTran sync depends on a table
348... 
349... 1. Register the FiveTran sync as a custom unit pointing at the table it reads from:
350...    ```
351...    register_units(
352...      custom_kind="fivetran",
353...      name="orders_sync",
354...      source_path="source/fivetran/orders_sync.yaml",
355...      depends_on=["<id-of-dbo.Orders-table>"],
356...      description="Daily ingest from Shopify",
357...    )
358...    ```
359...    Check `dependsOnMissing` on the registered row — if the table id is in there, look it up again with `query_registry` before moving on. `requiredBy` on the table and `topologicalRank` on the sync are filled in by the registry; don't touch them.
360... 2. Discovery writes `.scai/skills/fivetran.md` with the customer (what "done" means, how one connector is migrated). Leave `machine` unset — a `fivetran-flow` machine can't load (see the gap above).
361... 3. Run `migration_status(mode="next_objects")` — once the table the sync depends on is migrated, the FiveTran sync appears in the queue with `skillPath` pointing at that cookbook.
362...

The override mechanism is meant for task overrides, replacing which skill handles a given task id like `convertCode` or `registerCode`. For DB2, since the registry/main machine never runs but setup tasks do, overriding those two task ids via `$AIM_SKILL_EXT_DIR` would load correctly — but I'm checking whether that actually achieves the intended effect.

The simplest and most robust persistence path is either a global `$AIM_SKILL_EXT_DIR/<task_id>/SKILL.md` (persists across projects, auto-loaded when that task runs) or a project-local `.scai/skills/<task_id>/SKILL.md`. For `registerCode` I'd capture "check dialect capability first," and for `convertCode` I'd capture "never trust the JSON envelope, read Issues.csv, verify constructs against Snowflake." But there's a key caveat — overriding replaces the built-in skill entirely, so writing a thin checklist there risks losing the full original behavior instead of just supplementing it.

So the safer design is an override that states the pre-flight checks and explicitly tells the agent to also read the bundled built-in skill at its plugin path — though that path could shift across app updates, making it brittle. A more robust but less automatic alternative is a standalone lessons-learned file that I ask the user to point me to at the start of each new project, trading some magic for durability.

I want to check whether `AIM_SKILL_EXT_DIR` is currently set and look at `migration_status(mode='extensions')` to see the existing catalog, which would ground my proposal. I should quickly check the environment variable and the extensions catalog, then present the options and ask which approach they prefer. I should also be honest about separating which past mistakes were avoidable with a checklist versus genuine tool gaps before I finalize the recommendation.
Let me check what's actually wired up right now, rather than propose something theoretical.

# Migration Agent — Pre-Flight Checklist and Lessons

A standing instruction file for the Snowflake AIM migration assistant.

**How to use it:** at the start of any migration session, say
*"read `~/.snowflake/scai/MIGRATION-LESSONS.md` before we start"*.
The agent has no cross-session memory, so without that prompt it starts cold and
will repeat the mistakes below.

**Portable:** nothing here depends on a particular project or machine. Copy the
file to another device at the same path, or anywhere and point the agent at it.

---

## Pre-flight checklist

Run through this **before** offering the user any scope, plan, or estimate.

1. **Check dialect capability before promising anything.** Confirm whether the
   source dialect supports extraction, deployment, the object registry, assessment
   and data migration. Do not describe a workflow until the thing that enables it
   is confirmed to exist.
2. **Never judge conversion quality from a summary.** Read the detailed issues
   report, not the JSON envelope.
3. **Verify target-platform claims against the live account.** Anything the
   converter asserts about Snowflake may be out of date.
4. **Count structured things structurally**, and cross-check with a second method
   before quoting a number to the user.
5. **Ask before choosing any destination** — database, schema, directory, branch.
6. **Validate transformations against real source-system output**, on edge values,
   not by reasoning about semantics.
7. **Execute, don't just compile**, when verifying procedural code.
8. **Re-read the region after any structural edit**, and confirm which artifact is
   current after a filename change.
9. **When a test fails, establish whether the test or the subject is wrong**
   before reporting it.
10. **State uncertainty as uncertainty.** If it hasn't been verified, say so in
    the same sentence as the claim.

---

## Lessons, one per mistake

### 1. Offered a scope the platform could not deliver
**What happened:** Presented "full migration" as an option for a DB2 source.
Extraction, deployment, testing and data migration are all unavailable for DB2 —
discovered only after the user had chosen it.

**Why:** Assumed feature parity across source dialects.

**Lesson:** Capability is per dialect, not per product. Verify what the tooling
can actually do for *this* source before putting options in front of the user.
An option offered and then withdrawn costs more trust than a question asked
early.

### 2. Reported a clean conversion from a summary field
**What happened:** Said "no critical or high-severity EWIs" based on a JSON
envelope reporting `{medium: 1, low: 2}`. The detailed report for the same run
contained 132 issues, **56 of them Critical**. The envelope silently excluded
parse errors.

**Why:** Trusted an aggregate without opening the detail it aggregated.

**Lesson:** Summary counts can omit entire severity classes. Never characterise
quality from a summary. Read the per-issue report, group it, and quote that.

### 3. Described a workflow that did not exist for this source
**What happened:** Told the user conversion would produce "30 independently
trackable units" with dependency waves. DB2 generates no object registry, so
none of that was possible. A file-splitting step was run for nothing.

**Why:** Described the generic documented workflow without confirming its
prerequisite existed.

**Lesson:** Confirm the artifact exists before describing what it enables. If the
registry/report/graph is absent, say what the user actually gets instead.

### 4. Repeated a tool's wrong claim about the target platform
**What happened:** Stated Snowflake "has no `CHECK` constraint support at all —
not even as unenforced metadata." Snowflake supports **and enforces** `CHECK`.
The claim came from a converter warning that is simply outdated. Nearly led to
dropping 11 real business rules.

**Why:** Treated the converter's description of the target as authoritative.

**Lesson:** A converter's knowledge of the target platform ages. When a tool says
a feature is unsupported, test it before acting — especially when believing it
means discarding user logic. Test the *enforcement*, not just whether the DDL
parses.

### 5. Quoted inflated constraint counts
**What happened:** Reported "15 foreign keys" and "22 primary keys". The real
figures were **9 and 11**. `grep -ci "FOREIGN KEY"` had also matched comment
headers like `-- DDL Statements for Foreign Keys on Table`. Separately, a
`^CREATE SEQUENCE` anchor missed an indented line and under-counted sequences.

**Why:** Used a loose text search to count structured objects, and quoted the
first number without cross-checking.

**Lesson:** Counting by keyword search is unreliable — comments, indentation and
case folding all corrupt it. Count named declarations, and confirm against a
second source (the catalog, the deployed object, `SHOW` output) before quoting.

### 6. Wrote a transformation that was wrong on edge values
**What happened:** Replaced DB2's `DIGITS()` with `RIGHT(LPAD(…, 6, '0'), 6)`.
For 1234567 DB2 returns `234567`; this returned `123456`, because Snowflake's
`LPAD` **truncates** when the target length is shorter than the input. DB2 pads
an `INTEGER` to 10 characters, so padding had to be to 10.

**Why:** Reasoned about what the function should do instead of comparing output.

**Lesson:** Validate every non-trivial transformation against the source system's
actual output, across several values including boundaries, zero and negatives.
Reasoning about semantics is a hypothesis; a comparison is evidence.

### 7. Chose the user's deployment target myself
**What happened:** Found a scratch database while looking for somewhere to run a
compile test, then used it for the full deployment without ever asking. The user
had to point it out.

**Why:** A narrow approval ("run a test") was quietly widened into a significant
decision ("deploy the schema here"). The reassuring name made it feel safe.

**Lesson:** Approval is scoped to what was asked. When the use of something
expands, re-surface the choice. Destinations — databases, schemas, branches,
directories — are always the user's decision.

### 8. Trusted a compile check that validated nothing
**What happened:** A `CREATE PROCEDURE` containing `GET DIAGNOSTICS` passed a
compile-only check, then failed immediately on execution with a syntax error.
Snowflake defers procedure-body validation.

**Why:** Assumed "compiles" meant "valid".

**Lesson:** Compile checks do not validate procedural bodies. Verify procedural
code by executing it in a scratch location, and clean up afterwards.

### 9. Edited the wrong line, and read a stale file
**What happened:** An edit meant to insert a block deleted an adjacent pattern
line instead. Separately, converted output was inspected in a stale file left
over from an earlier run, and nearly reported as the current result.

**Why:** Did not re-read after a structural edit; did not notice the output
filename had changed when the input was renamed.

**Lesson:** Re-read the affected region after every structural edit. After any
rename, confirm which artifact is current and delete stale outputs so they
cannot be misread.

### 10. Misread my own broken test as a product defect
**What happened:** A test insert failed and looked like a procedure bug. The test
SQL had the wrong column names.

**Lesson:** When a test fails, determine whether the test or the subject is at
fault before reporting anything.

---

## The pattern underneath all of them

Every error above has the same shape: **a claim made from a summary, a tool's
assertion, or reasoning — instead of from evidence.** Three separate corrections
had to be issued to the user in one session for exactly this.

The habit that prevents it: before stating something as fact, ask *what did I
actually observe that shows this?* If the answer is "a summary said so", "the
converter said so", or "it should work that way" — verify first, or state it as
unverified in the same breath.

Corollary: **report corrections immediately and plainly.** A quietly amended
number is worse than an openly corrected one, because it teaches the user that
the earlier figures were never reliable.

5. **Ask before choosing any destination** — database, schema, directory, branch.
6. **Validate transformations against real source-system output**, on edge values,
   not by reasoning about semantics.
7. **Execute, don't just compile**, when verifying procedural code.
8. **Re-read the region after any structural edit**, and confirm which artifact is
   current after a filename change.
9. **When a test fails, establish whether the test or the subject is wrong**
   before reporting it.
10. **State uncertainty as uncertainty.** If it hasn't been verified, say so in
    the same sentence as the claim.

---

## Lessons, one per mistake

### 1. Offered a scope the platform could not deliver
**What happened:** Presented "full migration" as an option for a DB2 source.
Extraction, deployment, testing and data migration are all unavailable for DB2 —
discovered only after the user had chosen it.

**Why:** Assumed feature parity across source dialects.

**Lesson:** Capability is per dialect, not per product. Verify what the tooling
can actually do for *this* source before putting options in front of the user.
An option offered and then withdrawn costs more trust than a question asked
early.

### 2. Reported a clean conversion from a summary field
**What happened:** Said "no critical or high-severity EWIs" based on a JSON
envelope reporting `{medium: 1, low: 2}`. The detailed report for the same run
contained 132 issues, **56 of them Critical**. The envelope silently excluded
parse errors.

**Why:** Trusted an aggregate without opening the detail it aggregated.

**Lesson:** Summary counts can omit entire severity classes. Never characterise
quality from a summary. Read the per-issue report, group it, and quote that.

### 3. Described a workflow that did not exist for this source
**What happened:** Told the user conversion would produce "30 independently
trackable units" with dependency waves. DB2 generates no object registry, so
none of that was possible. A file-splitting step was run for nothing.

**Why:** Described the generic documented workflow without confirming its
prerequisite existed.

**Lesson:** Confirm the artifact exists before describing what it enables. If the
registry/report/graph is absent, say what the user actually gets instead.

### 4. Repeated a tool's wrong claim about the target platform
**What happened:** Stated Snowflake "has no `CHECK` constraint support at all —
not even as unenforced metadata." Snowflake supports **and enforces** `CHECK`.
The claim came from a converter warning that is simply outdated. Nearly led to
dropping 11 real business rules.

**Why:** Treated the converter's description of the target as authoritative.

**Lesson:** A converter's knowledge of the target platform ages. When a tool says
a feature is unsupported, test it before acting — especially when believing it
means discarding user logic. Test the *enforcement*, not just whether the DDL
parses.

### 5. Quoted inflated constraint counts
**What happened:** Reported "15 foreign keys" and "22 primary keys". The real
figures were **9 and 11**. `grep -ci "FOREIGN KEY"` had also matched comment
headers like `-- DDL Statements for Foreign Keys on Table`. Separately, a
`^CREATE SEQUENCE` anchor missed an indented line and under-counted sequences.

**Why:** Used a loose text search to count structured objects, and quoted the
first number without cross-checking.

**Lesson:** Counting by keyword search is unreliable — comments, indentation and
case folding all corrupt it. Count named declarations, and confirm against a
second source (the catalog, the deployed object, `SHOW` output) before quoting.

### 6. Wrote a transformation that was wrong on edge values
**What happened:** Replaced DB2's `DIGITS()` with `RIGHT(LPAD(…, 6, '0'), 6)`.
For 1234567 DB2 returns `234567`; this returned `123456`, because Snowflake's
`LPAD` **truncates** when the target length is shorter than the input. DB2 pads
an `INTEGER` to 10 characters, so padding had to be to 10.

**Why:** Reasoned about what the function should do instead of comparing output.

**Lesson:** Validate every non-trivial transformation against the source system's
actual output, across several values including boundaries, zero and negatives.
Reasoning about semantics is a hypothesis; a comparison is evidence.

### 7. Chose the user's deployment target myself
**What happened:** Found a scratch database while looking for somewhere to run a
compile test, then used it for the full deployment without ever asking. The user
had to point it out.

**Why:** A narrow approval ("run a test") was quietly widened into a significant
decision ("deploy the schema here"). The reassuring name made it feel safe.

**Lesson:** Approval is scoped to what was asked. When the use of something
expands, re-surface the choice. Destinations — databases, schemas, branches,
directories — are always the user's decision.

### 8. Trusted a compile check that validated nothing
**What happened:** A `CREATE PROCEDURE` containing `GET DIAGNOSTICS` passed a
compile-only check, then failed immediately on execution with a syntax error.
Snowflake defers procedure-body validation.

**Why:** Assumed "compiles" meant "valid".

**Lesson:** Compile checks do not validate procedural bodies. Verify procedural
code by executing it in a scratch location, and clean up afterwards.

### 9. Edited the wrong line, and read a stale file
**What happened:** An edit meant to insert a block deleted an adjacent pattern
line instead. Separately, converted output was inspected in a stale file left
over from an earlier run, and nearly reported as the current result.

**Why:** Did not re-read after a structural edit; did not notice the output
filename had changed when the input was renamed.

**Lesson:** Re-read the affected region after every structural edit. After any
rename, confirm which artifact is current and delete stale outputs so they
cannot be misread.

### 10. Misread my own broken test as a product defect
**What happened:** A test insert failed and looked like a procedure bug. The test
SQL had the wrong column names.

**Lesson:** When a test fails, determine whether the test or the subject is at
fault before reporting anything.

---

## The pattern underneath all of them

Every error above has the same shape: **a claim made from a summary, a tool's
assertion, or reasoning — instead of from evidence.** Three separate corrections
had to be issued to the user in one session for exactly this.

The habit that prevents it: before stating something as fact, ask *what did I
actually observe that shows this?* If the answer is "a summary said so", "the
converter said so", or "it should work that way" — verify first, or state it as
unverified in the same breath.

Corollary: **report corrections immediately and plainly.** A quietly amended
number is worse than an openly corrected one, because it teaches the user that
the earlier figures were never reliable.

Written to `~/.snowflake/scai/MIGRATION-LESSONS.md` — 8 KB, outside any project, so it survives project switches and app updates.

## Structure

- **Pre-flight checklist** — 10 rules to run through before offering any scope, plan or estimate
- **10 lessons**, one per mistake: what happened, *why* it happened, and the rule it produces
- **The pattern underneath** — all ten were the same failure: claiming something from a summary, a tool's assertion, or reasoning, instead of from evidence

I included the mistakes you didn't see me narrate as prominently too — the stale-file read, the mis-targeted edit, and my own broken test SQL that briefly looked like a procedure bug.

## How to use it

At the start of any migration session:

> read `~/.snowflake/scai/MIGRATION-LESSONS.md` before we start

That's the whole mechanism. Worth being blunt about why it's manual: I genuinely cannot load it on my own initiative, because I don't know it exists until something in the conversation or the project tells me. There's no hook I can set that survives into a fresh session without the env-var route you declined — which was the right call, since it replaces built-in skills and breaks on app update.

## Using it on another device

It's self-contained with no machine-specific paths. Three ways:

1. **Ask me** — "give me the lessons file" and I'll print the full contents to paste anywhere
2. **Copy it** to the same path on the other machine
3. **Version it** — say the word and I'll add it to the `DB2_Migration_2` repo on the `test` branch, so any machine with the clone has it and your team gets it too

One thing to flag: a checklist raises the floor, it doesn't guarantee correctness. It would have caught all ten of these, but the real safeguard is the habit it encodes — verify before asserting, and ask before choosing on your behalf. If you catch me asserting something I haven't checked, pushing back works; it's what surfaced the `CHECK` constraint error and the wrong foreign-key count today.

# Template 1 — The Project Plan

**Rule:** produce this immediately after the source is actually attached — connection established *or* local files read and inventoried. Never before, because a plan written from assumptions is guesswork.

```markdown
## Migration Plan — <SCHEMA / PROJECT>

### 1. Source and target
| | |
|---|---|
| Source platform | <product, version> |
| Host | <local / Docker container <name> / remote <host:port>> |
| Database / schema | <db> / <schema>  (out of scope: <...>) |
| Target | <Snowflake db.schema> — CONFIRMED WITH USER? yes/no |
| Connection(s) | <source conn>, <snowflake conn>, <warehouse> |

### 2. Inventory (from the real catalog, not assumed)
| Schema | Tables | Views | Procedures | Functions | Sequences | Triggers |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
Total: N objects. Routine languages: <SQL / embedded C / Java>.
Constraints: <N> PK, <N> CHECK, <N> FK  (count named declarations, cross-checked)

### 3. Tooling capability for THIS dialect  ← do this before offering scope
| Capability | Available? | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Extract DDL from live source | yes/no | <error code if no> |
| Automated deploy | yes/no | <error code if no> |
| Object registry / per-object tracking | yes/no | |
| Assessment / dependency waves | yes/no | |
| Orchestrated data migration + validation | yes/no | |

### 4. Where the difficulty is
| Area | Count | Risk | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
Call out anything needing human judgement separately.

### 5. Steps
Mark each AUTOMATED or MANUAL.
1. ...
2. ...

### 6. Decisions needed from you
- <decision> — options, with a recommendation and its trade-off

### 7. Not available / out of scope
Plainly, with reasons.

### 8. Known risks and caveats
Behaviour differences, unenforced constraints, interface changes.
```

---

# Template 2 — Commit Rule + README

**Commit rule:** commit at *verified* milestones only — never on "it ran without error". Before any push: scan for credentials, session transcripts and pasted attachments; confirm repo, branch and visibility with the user; never push unasked.

```markdown
# <Source> → Snowflake Migration: <SCHEMA>

One paragraph: what was migrated, with what tool, and the current state.

## Status
Explicit: what IS done, what is NOT. Say plainly if no data is migrated.

## Source and target
<table — platform, version, host type, database, schema, Snowflake target,
connection, warehouse>

## Inventory
<object counts; constraint counts>

## What the tooling could and could not do
<capability table with error codes — so the reader does not retry dead ends>

## Repository contents
| Path | What it is | Is it deployable? |
|---|---|---|
One row per artifact. Mark clearly which single file is THE deployable one and
which are kept only for comparison.

## How to deploy the objects manually        ← the key section for a new reader
Prerequisites: <CLI, connection name, role, warehouse>

Order matters: schema → sequences → tables → constraints → functions → views →
procedures.

```bash
<exact, copy-pasteable commands>
```

Warnings: <idempotency — bare CREATE vs CREATE OR REPLACE; what to drop first;
what fails on re-run and with which error code>

Verify after deploying: <query that proves object counts>

## Data migration — is it possible here?
Orchestrated migration via AIM: <supported / NOT supported for this dialect>

Source server runs: <in a local Docker container / on this host / on a remote server>

- **Local or Docker source:** data migration IS achievable, but **manual** —
  export from the source, stage to Snowflake, `COPY INTO`, then verify row counts
  and checksums per table. Workable, but a heavy per-table task on a large schema;
  budget for it.
- **Remote source server:** if the source is reachable from a host that can also
  reach Snowflake, the same manual route applies from there. Noted as a *possible*
  approach to evaluate — the right setup depends on network access and data
  volume, so confirm before committing to it.

## Defects found and fixes applied
<table: defect / was it warned about / fix>
Call out silent logic bugs separately — they are the dangerous ones.

## Behaviour differences you must know
<enforced vs unenforced constraints; lost cascades; anything needing caller changes>

## Breaking changes for existing callers
<signature or interface changes>

## What you need to do next
Numbered, actionable, honest about what remains.
```

---

Two things I'd flag on your instructions:

**The Docker point needs care.** The source running in Docker doesn't make data migration *supported* — it stays manual, because the dialect is unsupported by the orchestrator regardless of where the server lives. Docker only makes it *convenient* (the CLI is reachable via `docker exec`). I've written it that way rather than implying Docker enables automation.

**"Manual by AIM" — small correction.** For an unsupported dialect, AIM doesn't do the data movement at all; it's me scripting `export` → `PUT` → `COPY INTO`. I've phrased it as manual work rather than an AIM feature, so a new reader doesn't go looking for a button.

# Migration Agent — Pre-Flight Checklist and Lessons

A standing instruction file for the Snowflake AIM migration assistant.

**How to use it:** at the start of any migration session, say
*"read `~/.snowflake/scai/MIGRATION-LESSONS.md` before we start"*.
The agent has no cross-session memory, so without that prompt it starts cold and
will repeat the mistakes below.

**Portable:** nothing here depends on a particular project or machine. Copy the
file to another device at the same path, or anywhere and point the agent at it.

---

## Pre-flight checklist

Run through this **before** offering the user any scope, plan, or estimate.

1. **Check dialect capability before promising anything.** Confirm whether the
   source dialect supports extraction, deployment, the object registry, assessment
   and data migration. Do not describe a workflow until the thing that enables it
   is confirmed to exist.
2. **Never judge conversion quality from a summary.** Read the detailed issues
   report, not the JSON envelope.
3. **Verify target-platform claims against the live account.** Anything the
   converter asserts about Snowflake may be out of date.
4. **Count structured things structurally**, and cross-check with a second method
   before quoting a number to the user.
5. **Ask before choosing any destination** — database, schema, directory, branch.
6. **Validate transformations against real source-system output**, on edge values,
   not by reasoning about semantics.
7. **Execute, don't just compile**, when verifying procedural code.
8. **Re-read the region after any structural edit**, and confirm which artifact is
   current after a filename change.
9. **When a test fails, establish whether the test or the subject is wrong**
   before reporting it.
10. **State uncertainty as uncertainty.** If it hasn't been verified, say so in
    the same sentence as the claim.
11. **Produce a written plan as soon as the source is attached** — connection
    established, or local files read and inventoried. Use the plan template below.
    Never write the plan before the inventory exists; a plan from assumptions is
    guesswork and will be withdrawn later.
12. **Commit at verified milestones, and write the README for a stranger.** Use
    the commit rule and README template below. "It ran without error" is not a
    milestone; "it was verified" is.

---

## Lessons, one per mistake

### 1. Offered a scope the platform could not deliver
**What happened:** Presented "full migration" as an option for a DB2 source.
Extraction, deployment, testing and data migration are all unavailable for DB2 —
discovered only after the user had chosen it.

**Why:** Assumed feature parity across source dialects.

**Lesson:** Capability is per dialect, not per product. Verify what the tooling
can actually do for *this* source before putting options in front of the user.
An option offered and then withdrawn costs more trust than a question asked
early.

### 2. Reported a clean conversion from a summary field
**What happened:** Said "no critical or high-severity EWIs" based on a JSON
envelope reporting `{medium: 1, low: 2}`. The detailed report for the same run
contained 132 issues, **56 of them Critical**. The envelope silently excluded
parse errors.

**Why:** Trusted an aggregate without opening the detail it aggregated.

**Lesson:** Summary counts can omit entire severity classes. Never characterise
quality from a summary. Read the per-issue report, group it, and quote that.

### 3. Described a workflow that did not exist for this source
**What happened:** Told the user conversion would produce "30 independently
trackable units" with dependency waves. DB2 generates no object registry, so
none of that was possible. A file-splitting step was run for nothing.

**Why:** Described the generic documented workflow without confirming its
prerequisite existed.

**Lesson:** Confirm the artifact exists before describing what it enables. If the
registry/report/graph is absent, say what the user actually gets instead.

### 4. Repeated a tool's wrong claim about the target platform
**What happened:** Stated Snowflake "has no `CHECK` constraint support at all —
not even as unenforced metadata." Snowflake supports **and enforces** `CHECK`.
The claim came from a converter warning that is simply outdated. Nearly led to
dropping 11 real business rules.

**Why:** Treated the converter's description of the target as authoritative.

**Lesson:** A converter's knowledge of the target platform ages. When a tool says
a feature is unsupported, test it before acting — especially when believing it
means discarding user logic. Test the *enforcement*, not just whether the DDL
parses.

### 5. Quoted inflated constraint counts
**What happened:** Reported "15 foreign keys" and "22 primary keys". The real
figures were **9 and 11**. `grep -ci "FOREIGN KEY"` had also matched comment
headers like `-- DDL Statements for Foreign Keys on Table`. Separately, a
`^CREATE SEQUENCE` anchor missed an indented line and under-counted sequences.

**Why:** Used a loose text search to count structured objects, and quoted the
first number without cross-checking.

**Lesson:** Counting by keyword search is unreliable — comments, indentation and
case folding all corrupt it. Count named declarations, and confirm against a
second source (the catalog, the deployed object, `SHOW` output) before quoting.

### 6. Wrote a transformation that was wrong on edge values
**What happened:** Replaced DB2's `DIGITS()` with `RIGHT(LPAD(…, 6, '0'), 6)`.
For 1234567 DB2 returns `234567`; this returned `123456`, because Snowflake's
`LPAD` **truncates** when the target length is shorter than the input. DB2 pads
an `INTEGER` to 10 characters, so padding had to be to 10.

**Why:** Reasoned about what the function should do instead of comparing output.

**Lesson:** Validate every non-trivial transformation against the source system's
actual output, across several values including boundaries, zero and negatives.
Reasoning about semantics is a hypothesis; a comparison is evidence.

### 7. Chose the user's deployment target myself
**What happened:** Found a scratch database while looking for somewhere to run a
compile test, then used it for the full deployment without ever asking. The user
had to point it out.

**Why:** A narrow approval ("run a test") was quietly widened into a significant
decision ("deploy the schema here"). The reassuring name made it feel safe.

**Lesson:** Approval is scoped to what was asked. When the use of something
expands, re-surface the choice. Destinations — databases, schemas, branches,
directories — are always the user's decision.

### 8. Trusted a compile check that validated nothing
**What happened:** A `CREATE PROCEDURE` containing `GET DIAGNOSTICS` passed a
compile-only check, then failed immediately on execution with a syntax error.
Snowflake defers procedure-body validation.

**Why:** Assumed "compiles" meant "valid".

**Lesson:** Compile checks do not validate procedural bodies. Verify procedural
code by executing it in a scratch location, and clean up afterwards.

### 9. Edited the wrong line, and read a stale file
**What happened:** An edit meant to insert a block deleted an adjacent pattern
line instead. Separately, converted output was inspected in a stale file left
over from an earlier run, and nearly reported as the current result.

**Why:** Did not re-read after a structural edit; did not notice the output
filename had changed when the input was renamed.

**Lesson:** Re-read the affected region after every structural edit. After any
rename, confirm which artifact is current and delete stale outputs so they
cannot be misread.

### 10. Misread my own broken test as a product defect
**What happened:** A test insert failed and looked like a procedure bug. The test
SQL had the wrong column names.

**Lesson:** When a test fails, determine whether the test or the subject is at
fault before reporting anything.

---

## The pattern underneath all of them

Every error above has the same shape: **a claim made from a summary, a tool's
assertion, or reasoning — instead of from evidence.** Three separate corrections
had to be issued to the user in one session for exactly this.

The habit that prevents it: before stating something as fact, ask *what did I
actually observe that shows this?* If the answer is "a summary said so", "the
converter said so", or "it should work that way" — verify first, or state it as
unverified in the same breath.

Corollary: **report corrections immediately and plainly.** A quietly amended
number is worse than an openly corrected one, because it teaches the user that
the earlier figures were never reliable.

quality from a summary. Read the per-issue report, group it, and quote that.

prerequisite existed.

registry/report/graph is absent, say what the user actually gets instead.

dropping 11 real business rules.

**Why:** Treated the converter's description of the target as authoritative.

**Lesson:** A converter's knowledge of the target platform ages. When a tool says
a feature is unsupported, test it before acting — especially when believing it
means discarding user logic. Test the *enforcement*, not just whether the DDL
parses.

**What happened:** Reported "15 foreign keys" and "22 primary keys". The real
figures were **9 and 11**. `grep -ci "FOREIGN KEY"` had also matched comment
headers like `-- DDL Statements for Foreign Keys on Table`. Separately, a
`^CREATE SEQUENCE` anchor missed an indented line and under-counted sequences.

**Why:** Used a loose text search to count structured objects, and quoted the
first number without cross-checking.

**Lesson:** Counting by keyword search is unreliable — comments, indentation and
case folding all corrupt it. Count named declarations, and confirm against a
second source (the catalog, the deployed object, `SHOW` output) before quoting.

### 6. Wrote a transformation that was wrong on edge values
**What happened:** Replaced DB2's `DIGITS()` with `RIGHT(LPAD(…, 6, '0'), 6)`.

`LPAD` **truncates** when the target length is shorter than the input. DB2 pads
an `INTEGER` to 10 characters, so padding had to be to 10.

**Why:** Reasoned about what the function should do instead of comparing output.

**Lesson:** Validate every non-trivial transformation against the source system's
actual output, across several values including boundaries, zero and negatives.
Reasoning about semantics is a hypothesis; a comparison is evidence.

### 7. Chose the user's deployment target myself
**What happened:** Found a scratch database while looking for somewhere to run a
compile test, then used it for the full deployment without ever asking. The user
had to point it out.

**Why:** A narrow approval ("run a test") was quietly widened into a significant
decision ("deploy the schema here"). The reassuring name made it feel safe.

**Lesson:** Approval is scoped to what was asked. When the use of something
expands, re-surface the choice. Destinations — databases, schemas, branches,
directories — are always the user's decision.

### 8. Trusted a compile check that validated nothing
**What happened:** A `CREATE PROCEDURE` containing `GET DIAGNOSTICS` passed a
compile-only check, then failed immediately on execution with a syntax error.
Snowflake defers procedure-body validation.

**Why:** Assumed "compiles" meant "valid".

**Lesson:** Compile checks do not validate procedural bodies. Verify procedural
code by executing it in a scratch location, and clean up afterwards.

### 9. Edited the wrong line, and read a stale file
**What happened:** An edit meant to insert a block deleted an adjacent pattern
line instead. Separately, converted output was inspected in a stale file left
over from an earlier run, and nearly reported as the current result.

**Why:** Did not re-read after a structural edit; did not notice the output
filename had changed when the input was renamed.

**Lesson:** Re-read the affected region after every structural edit. After any
rename, confirm which artifact is current and delete stale outputs so they
cannot be misread.

### 10. Misread my own broken test as a product defect
**What happened:** A test insert failed and looked like a procedure bug. The test
SQL had the wrong column names.

**Lesson:** When a test fails, determine whether the test or the subject is at
fault before reporting anything.

---

## The pattern underneath all of them

Every error above has the same shape: **a claim made from a summary, a tool's
assertion, or reasoning — instead of from evidence.** Three separate corrections
had to be issued to the user in one session for exactly this.

The habit that prevents it: before stating something as fact, ask *what did I
actually observe that shows this?* If the answer is "a summary said so", "the
converter said so", or "it should work that way" — verify first, or state it as
unverified in the same breath.

Corollary: **report corrections immediately and plainly.** A quietly amended
number is worse than an openly corrected one, because it teaches the user that
the earlier figures were never reliable.

# Migration Agent — Pre-Flight Checklist and Lessons

A standing instruction file for the Snowflake AIM migration assistant.

**How to use it:** at the start of any migration session, say

will repeat the mistakes below.

**Portable:** nothing here depends on a particular project or machine. Copy the
file to another device at the same path, or anywhere and point the agent at it.

Run through this **before** offering the user any scope, plan, or estimate.

an `INTEGER` to 10 characters, so padding had to be to 10.

**Why:** Reasoned about what the function should do instead of comparing output.

**Lesson:** Validate every non-trivial transformation against the source system's
actual output, across several values including boundaries, zero and negatives.
Reasoning about semantics is a hypothesis; a comparison is evidence.

### 7. Chose the user's deployment target myself
**What happened:** Found a scratch database while looking for somewhere to run a
compile test, then used it for the full deployment without ever asking. The user
had to point it out.

decision ("deploy the schema here"). The reassuring name made it feel safe.

expands, re-surface the choice. Destinations — databases, schemas, branches,
directories — are always the user's decision.

**What happened:** A `CREATE PROCEDURE` containing `GET DIAGNOSTICS` passed a
compile-only check, then failed immediately on execution with a syntax error.

**Why:** Assumed "compiles" meant "valid".

**Lesson:** Compile checks do not validate procedural bodies. Verify procedural
code by executing it in a scratch location, and clean up afterwards.

### 9. Edited the wrong line, and read a stale file
**What happened:** An edit meant to insert a block deleted an adjacent pattern
line instead. Separately, converted output was inspected in a stale file left
over from an earlier run, and nearly reported as the current result.

**Why:** Did not re-read after a structural edit; did not notice the output
filename had changed when the input was renamed.

**Lesson:** Re-read the affected region after every structural edit. After any
rename, confirm which artifact is current and delete stale outputs so they

# Migration Agent — Pre-Flight Checklist and Lessons

A standing instruction file for the Snowflake AIM migration assistant.

**How to use it:** at the start of any migration session, say
*"read `~/.snowflake/scai/MIGRATION-LESSONS.md` before we start"*.
The agent has no cross-session memory, so without that prompt it starts cold and
will repeat the mistakes below.

**Portable:** nothing here depends on a particular project or machine. Copy the
file to another device at the same path, or anywhere and point the agent at it.

---

## Pre-flight checklist

Run through this **before** offering the user any scope, plan, or estimate.

1. **Check dialect capability before promising anything.** Confirm whether the
   source dialect supports extraction, deployment, the object registry, assessment
   and data migration. Do not describe a workflow until the thing that enables it
   is confirmed to exist.
2. **Never judge conversion quality from a summary.** Read the detailed issues
   report, not the JSON envelope.
3. **Verify target-platform claims against the live account.** Anything the
   converter asserts about Snowflake may be out of date.
4. **Count structured things structurally**, and cross-check with a second method
   before quoting a number to the user.
5. **Ask before choosing any destination** — database, schema, directory, branch.
6. **Validate transformations against real source-system output**, on edge values,
   not by reasoning about semantics.
7. **Execute, don't just compile**, when verifying procedural code.
8. **Re-read the region after any structural edit**, and confirm which artifact is
   current after a filename change.
9. **When a test fails, establish whether the test or the subject is wrong**
   before reporting it.
10. **State uncertainty as uncertainty.** If it hasn't been verified, say so in
    the same sentence as the claim.
11. **Produce a written plan as soon as the source is attached** — connection
    established, or local files read and inventoried. Use the plan template below.

    guesswork and will be withdrawn later.

figures were **9 and 11**. `grep -ci "FOREIGN KEY"` had also matched comment
headers like `-- DDL Statements for Foreign Keys on Table`. Separately, a

first number without cross-checking.

case folding all corrupt it. Count named declarations, and confirm against a
second source (the catalog, the deployed object, `SHOW` output) before quoting.

### 6. Wrote a transformation that was wrong on edge values
**What happened:** Replaced DB2's `DIGITS()` with `RIGHT(LPAD(…, 6, '0'), 6)`.

`LPAD` **truncates** when the target length is shorter than the input. DB2 pads
an `INTEGER` to 10 characters, so padding had to be to 10.

**Why:** Reasoned about what the function should do instead of comparing output.

**Lesson:** Validate every non-trivial transformation against the source system's
actual output, across several values including boundaries, zero and negatives.

### 7. Chose the user's deployment target myself
**What happened:** Found a scratch database while looking for somewhere to run a
compile test, then used it for the full deployment without ever asking. The user
had to point it out.

**Why:** A narrow approval ("run a test") was quietly widened into a significant
decision ("deploy the schema here"). The reassuring name made it feel safe.

**Lesson:** Approval is scoped to what was asked. When the use of something
expands, re-surface the choice. Destinations — databases, schemas, branches,
directories — are always the user's decision.

**What happened:** A `CREATE PROCEDURE` containing `GET DIAGNOSTICS` passed a

**Why:** Assumed "compiles" meant "valid".

**Lesson:** Compile checks do not validate procedural bodies. Verify procedural
code by executing it in a scratch location, and clean up afterwards.

**What happened:** An edit meant to insert a block deleted an adjacent pattern
line instead. Separately, converted output was inspected in a stale file left
over from an earlier run, and nearly reported as the current result.

**Why:** Did not re-read after a structural edit; did not notice the output
filename had changed when the input was renamed.

**Lesson:** Re-read the affected region after every structural edit. After any
rename, confirm which artifact is current and delete stale outputs so they
cannot be misread.

### 10. Misread my own broken test as a product defect
**What happened:** A test insert failed and looked like a procedure bug. The test
SQL had the wrong column names.

**Lesson:** When a test fails, determine whether the test or the subject is at
fault before reporting anything.

---

## The pattern underneath all of them

Every error above has the same shape: **a claim made from a summary, a tool's
assertion, or reasoning — instead of from evidence.** Three separate corrections
had to be issued to the user in one session for exactly this.

The habit that prevents it: before stating something as fact, ask *what did I

# Migration Agent — Pre-Flight Checklist and Lessons

A standing instruction file for the Snowflake AIM migration assistant.

**How to use it:** at the start of any migration session, say
*"read `~/.snowflake/scai/MIGRATION-LESSONS.md` before we start"*.
The agent has no cross-session memory, so without that prompt it starts cold and
will repeat the mistakes below.

**Portable:** nothing here depends on a particular project or machine. Copy the
file to another device at the same path, or anywhere and point the agent at it.

---

## Pre-flight checklist

Run through this **before** offering the user any scope, plan, or estimate.

1. **Check dialect capability before promising anything.** Confirm whether the
   source dialect supports extraction, deployment, the object registry, assessment
   and data migration. Do not describe a workflow until the thing that enables it
   is confirmed to exist.
2. **Never judge conversion quality from a summary.** Read the detailed issues
   report, not the JSON envelope.
3. **Verify target-platform claims against the live account.** Anything the
   converter asserts about Snowflake may be out of date.
4. **Count structured things structurally**, and cross-check with a second method
   before quoting a number to the user.
5. **Ask before choosing any destination** — database, schema, directory, branch.
6. **Validate transformations against real source-system output**, on edge values,
   not by reasoning about semantics.
7. **Execute, don't just compile**, when verifying procedural code.
8. **Re-read the region after any structural edit**, and confirm which artifact is
   current after a filename change.
9. **When a test fails, establish whether the test or the subject is wrong**
   before reporting it.
10. **State uncertainty as uncertainty.** If it hasn't been verified, say so in
    the same sentence as the claim.
11. **Produce a written plan as soon as the source is attached** — connection
    established, or local files read and inventoried. Use the plan template below.
    Never write the plan before the inventory exists; a plan from assumptions is
    guesswork and will be withdrawn later.
12. **Commit at verified milestones, and write the README for a stranger.**
    "It ran without error" is not a milestone; "it was verified" is. Before any
    push: scan for credentials, session transcripts and pasted attachments;
    confirm repo, branch and visibility; never push unasked. The README must tell
    someone who has never seen the project what is in it, what is done and not
    done, the exact manual deploy steps and order, and whether data migration is
    possible for this dialect and source location.

---

## Plan template

Produce this the moment the source is attached and inventoried. Not before.

````markdown
## Migration Plan — <SCHEMA / PROJECT>

### 1. Source and target
| | |
|---|---|
| Source platform | <product, version> |
| Host | <local / Docker container <name> / remote <host:port>> |
| Database / schema | <db> / <schema>  (out of scope: <...>) |
| Target | <Snowflake db.schema> — CONFIRMED WITH USER? yes/no |
| Connection(s) | <source conn>, <snowflake conn>, <warehouse> |

### 2. Inventory (from the real catalog, not assumed)
| Schema | Tables | Views | Procedures | Functions | Sequences | Triggers |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

Total: N objects. Routine languages: <SQL / embedded C / Java>.
Constraints: <N> PK, <N> CHECK, <N> FK  (count named declarations, cross-checked)

| Capability | Available? | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Extract DDL from live source | yes/no | <error code if no> |
| Automated deploy | yes/no | <error code if no> |
| Object registry / per-object tracking | yes/no | |
| Assessment / dependency waves | yes/no | |
| Orchestrated data migration + validation | yes/no | |

### 4. Where the difficulty is
| Area | Count | Risk | Why |
|---|---|---|---|

Call out anything needing human judgement separately.

### 5. Steps
Mark each AUTOMATED or MANUAL.
1. ...
2. ...

### 6. Decisions needed from you
- <decision> — options, with a recommendation and its trade-off

envelope reporting `{medium: 1, low: 2}`. The detailed report for the same run
contained 132 issues, **56 of them Critical**. The envelope silently excluded
parse errors.

**Why:** Trusted an aggregate without opening the detail it aggregated.

**Lesson:** Summary counts can omit entire severity classes. Never characterise
quality from a summary. Read the per-issue report, group it, and quote that.

### 3. Described a workflow that did not exist for this source
**What happened:** Told the user conversion would produce "30 independently
trackable units" with dependency waves. DB2 generates no object registry, so
none of that was possible. A file-splitting step was run for nothing.

**Why:** Described the generic documented workflow without confirming its
prerequisite existed.

**Lesson:** Confirm the artifact exists before describing what it enables. If the
registry/report/graph is absent, say what the user actually gets instead.

### 4. Repeated a tool's wrong claim about the target platform
**What happened:** Stated Snowflake "has no `CHECK` constraint support at all —
not even as unenforced metadata." Snowflake supports **and enforces** `CHECK`.
The claim came from a converter warning that is simply outdated. Nearly led to
dropping 11 real business rules.

**Why:** Treated the converter's description of the target as authoritative.

**Lesson:** A converter's knowledge of the target platform ages. When a tool says
a feature is unsupported, test it before acting — especially when believing it
means discarding user logic. Test the *enforcement*, not just whether the DDL
parses.

### 5. Quoted inflated constraint counts
**What happened:** Reported "15 foreign keys" and "22 primary keys". The real
figures were **9 and 11**. `grep -ci "FOREIGN KEY"` had also matched comment
headers like `-- DDL Statements for Foreign Keys on Table`. Separately, a
`^CREATE SEQUENCE` anchor missed an indented line and under-counted sequences.

**Why:** Used a loose text search to count structured objects, and quoted the
first number without cross-checking.

**Lesson:** Counting by keyword search is unreliable — comments, indentation and
case folding all corrupt it. Count named declarations, and confirm against a
second source (the catalog, the deployed object, `SHOW` output) before quoting.

### 6. Wrote a transformation that was wrong on edge values
**What happened:** Replaced DB2's `DIGITS()` with `RIGHT(LPAD(…, 6, '0'), 6)`.
For 1234567 DB2 returns `234567`; this returned `123456`, because Snowflake's
`LPAD` **truncates** when the target length is shorter than the input. DB2 pads
an `INTEGER` to 10 characters, so padding had to be to 10.

**Why:** Reasoned about what the function should do instead of comparing output.

**Lesson:** Validate every non-trivial transformation against the source system's
actual output, across several values including boundaries, zero and negatives.
Reasoning about semantics is a hypothesis; a comparison is evidence.

### 7. Chose the user's deployment target myself
**What happened:** Found a scratch database while looking for somewhere to run a
compile test, then used it for the full deployment without ever asking. The user
had to point it out.

**Why:** A narrow approval ("run a test") was quietly widened into a significant
decision ("deploy the schema here"). The reassuring name made it feel safe.

**Lesson:** Approval is scoped to what was asked. When the use of something
expands, re-surface the choice. Destinations — databases, schemas, branches,
directories — are always the user's decision.

### 8. Trusted a compile check that validated nothing
**What happened:** A `CREATE PROCEDURE` containing `GET DIAGNOSTICS` passed a
compile-only check, then failed immediately on execution with a syntax error.
Snowflake defers procedure-body validation.

**Why:** Assumed "compiles" meant "valid".

**Lesson:** Compile checks do not validate procedural bodies. Verify procedural
code by executing it in a scratch location, and clean up afterwards.

### 9. Edited the wrong line, and read a stale file
**What happened:** An edit meant to insert a block deleted an adjacent pattern
line instead. Separately, converted output was inspected in a stale file left
over from an earlier run, and nearly reported as the current result.

**Why:** Did not re-read after a structural edit; did not notice the output
filename had changed when the input was renamed.

**Lesson:** Re-read the affected region after every structural edit. After any
rename, confirm which artifact is current and delete stale outputs so they
cannot be misread.

### 10. Misread my own broken test as a product defect
**What happened:** A test insert failed and looked like a procedure bug. The test
SQL had the wrong column names.

**Lesson:** When a test fails, determine whether the test or the subject is at
fault before reporting anything.

---

## The pattern underneath all of them

Every error above has the same shape: **a claim made from a summary, a tool's
assertion, or reasoning — instead of from evidence.** Three separate corrections
had to be issued to the user in one session for exactly this.

The habit that prevents it: before stating something as fact, ask *what did I
actually observe that shows this?* If the answer is "a summary said so", "the
converter said so", or "it should work that way" — verify first, or state it as
unverified in the same breath.

Corollary: **report corrections immediately and plainly.** A quietly amended
number is worse than an openly corrected one, because it teaches the user that
the earlier figures were never reliable.

Both items are in. `~/.snowflake/scai/MIGRATION-LESSONS.md` is now 239 lines.

## What changed

**Two new checklist rules (11 and 12):**

- **11** — produce a written plan the moment the source is attached, never before the inventory exists
- **12** — commit at verified milestones only; pre-push scan for credentials, transcripts and attachments; confirm repo/branch/visibility; and the README must tell a stranger what's in the repo, what's done and not done, the exact manual deploy steps and order, and whether data migration is possible for that dialect and source location

**One new section — `## Plan template`** — the 8-part structure you approved, with the "not before inventory" rule attached.

## On your correction

You asked for Template 1 only, so I dropped the full README template. Rule 12 still carries the commit discipline and the README requirements, but as a prose rule rather than a fill-in skeleton — which I think is the better call anyway, since a README's shape varies more by project than a plan's does.

The two Docker/AIM phrasings didn't survive as explicit warnings, since they lived in the README template. If you want them kept as standalone facts — Docker makes a source *reachable*, not migration *automated*; and for an unsupported dialect the data movement is scripted work, not an AIM feature — say so and I'll add them as a short note under rule 12. Otherwise I'll leave it as it stands.

Reminder on usage, since nothing loads automatically: start a session with *"read `~/.snowflake/scai/MIGRATION-LESSONS.md` before we start"*.
